title: The Surveyor Who Invented Modern India
event_summary: In April 1802, Colonel William Lambton began the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India from St. Thomas Mount near Madras, using a massive half-ton theodolite hauled across jungles and mountains. Over the next seven decades, Lambton and his successor Radhanath Sikdar — a Bengali mathematician — measured the entire subcontinent with unprecedented precision, ultimately proving that Peak XV (later named Everest) was the world's tallest mountain. Sikdar, a largely uncredited Indian computer, performed the decisive calculations in 1852 from a desk in Dehradun.
why_forgotten: The British credited the survey to its European directors, especially George Everest, while Sikdar's pivotal computational work was systematically downplayed in colonial records. The survey itself became so foundational to governance that it disappeared into bureaucratic invisibility — everyone used its maps, but few remembered the staggering human cost of the fieldwork, including hundreds of Indian surveyors who died from malaria, tiger attacks, and exposure.
why_it_matters: The Great Trigonometrical Survey created the mathematical skeleton upon which modern India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Myanmar were literally drawn — every border, railway, and administrative boundary traces back to its triangulation points. Sikdar's suppressed achievement symbolizes the uncredited intellectual labor of colonized peoples in building modern science, and the Survey of India he helped create remains the country's primary mapping authority today.
